text.p: The report of the House Industry Science and Tourism on Fair Trading tabled on Monday has the potential to emerge as one of the most important developments for Australian business for some years.
We say potential because it is yet to be seen whether, and to what degree, the Howard government will act on its recommendations.
In political terms it could certainly have a profound impact on the outcome of the next election.

The unanimous decision by the committee to recommend legislation to protect small business from the depredations of big business should come as no surprise to readers of Inside Canberra -- we forecast this on February 14.

The report found decisively on the two major issues -- firstly there is a huge problem of small business being dealt with unconscionably by big business and secondly, this situation cannot be addressed by voluntary codes of conduct -- legislative underpinning is necessary.
What is recommended is anything but a minimalist legislative approach. The major recommendations are:

-- the Unconscionable Conduct section of the Trade Practices Act to be amended to include a new section outlawing "unfair conduct", with an extensive list of factors courts may take into account in determining if commercial conduct is unfair;
-- a Uniform Retail Tenancy Code to be drafted in cooperation with the States and to be underpinned by the Trade Practices Act;

-- the Commonwealth to raise with the States through the Council of Australian Government the possibility of local planning authorities requiring social and economic impact statements to be lodged with development applications for new shopping centres with a view to restricting oversupply of floor space;
-- Commonwealth to enact franchising legislation covering all franchising arrangements including motor vehicle dealerships and the petroleum industry;
-- Small business representatives to be included in the Australian Banking Industry Ombudsman Scheme and any dispute resolution mechanisms established as a result of the Wallis inquiry;
-- Treasury to examine the impact on small business of securing small business loans against real assets, rather than the commercial viability of the small business.
The question is, what will the government do about the report? The first thing to be said is it is in no hurry to do anything.

In the House on Tuesday, Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser, after much ducking and weaving following a question from the Labor Shadow Small Business spokesman Steve Martin asking if the government would accept the report, said the government would give its reaction in three months.
It could hardly be said this amounts to a courteous recognition of the tabling of the report, let alone indicating the government is in any way appreciative of the need to act with some urgency.

The outcome of the House inquiry has been a triumph for the Small Business Coalition and the Motor Trades Association of Australia and the Pharmacy Guild of Australia in particular, firstly in securing from the former Liberal Federal Director, Andrew Robb, an undertaking in advance of the last election for a Parliamentary inquiry into Fair Trading and then in persuading the committee the legislative path is the way to go.
Other members of the Coalition who were advocating voluntary codes and no black letter law were decisively defeated, including the Victorian Employers' Chamber of Commerce and ACCI.

But the battle is not yet over -- arrayed against the committee's recommendations are powerful influences, apart from VECCI and ACCI -- the oil companies, shopping mall developers, major retailers, the banks, the car manufacturers and car importers (who would be required to join a franchising code) and last but not least Treasury and the Department of Industry Science and Tourism.
The small business sector is planning a massive lobbying campaign in support of the Fair Trading report and this will certainly be needed.

There is not a single minister in Cabinet who would support most of the recommendations of the committee. On the other hand the overwhelming majority of the backbench in both the Liberal and National Parties would strongly support the recommendations.

These were unanimous (except one Labor MP, Allan Morris, put in a minority report saying the recommendations did not go far enough) and came from a committee on which the coalition has a majority of members and ALL of them are former small business people.
It will not be easy for the government to tell the committee and the backbench they are all wrong.

Incidentally at the press conference launch of the report on Monday deputy chairman David Beddall pointed out the committee had challenged Treasury, which was all in favor of voluntary codes, to name one such code which had worked.
Beddall said this was two months ago and still there was no word from Treasury.
Despite this there is a view in the ministerial lobbies the government will stall any decision until next year and by then it will be too late to do anything before the next election.

If this is to be the case it would cause enormous electoral damage to Howard who continues to put himself forward, to an increasingly disbelieving audience, as the only true champion of small business.

Is he going to say, having come to power on the small business ticket, he will not legislate to protect small business because he doesn't believe in the government legislating and small business should look after itself with voluntary codes of conduct?
In our view, Howard will have to do something before the next election.
He can hardly hold out against legislating for a franchise code after the shambles created in franchising by Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser.
A Uniform Retail Tenancy Code is a goer if only because the Property Council of Australia (the old BOMA) is in favor of such a code.
The committee recommended the Australian Competition Consumer Commission (ACCC) draft the code for submission to the Council of Australian Governments.
Whether the ACCC could get anything like agreement on the detail is the question.

For example, small shopkeepers would certainly applaud the Security of Tenure provisions but mall owners would not -- minimum lease term of five years; sitting tenants to have the option of renewal for a further five years and sitting tenants to have the right of first refusal of the lease for a subsequent five year period.
Then there would hardly be agreement on compensation for the shopkeeper due to trading disturbance caused by redevelopment.

The recommendation which will meet the stiffest resistance is to amend Part 1VA of the Trade Practices Act ((Unconscionable Conduct) to include a new section proscribing "unfair conduct" with an extensive list of factors the courts may take into account in determining if commercial conduct is unfair.
Big business has already homed in on this saying it is far too broad, would apply to all business relationships and would cause great business uncertainty.
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273-1600
